periods.label: Old age

levels.sentence: When in 1775 I discoursed with Dr Johnson on old age, he said, 'they are always telling lies of us old fellows,' and asked whether I would know the evils of age by having the gout and decrepitude.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1775, the conversation happening to turn upon old age, Dr Johnson fell into a strain of earnest reflection. 'Ay, Sir,' said he, 'they are always telling lies of us old fellows.' I was perhaps too forward in asking what it was to feel the evils of that state, for he immediately replied, 'What, Sir, would you know what it is to feel the evils of old age? Would you have the gout? Would you have decrepitude?' His reproof was just; for there is no knowledge of age but in age itself, and to desire it is to desire suffering.
levels.summary:
In 1775 I sat with Dr Johnson while the talk fell upon old age, a subject on which he could speak with singular authority, being himself advanced in years.

He first complained, 'they are always telling lies of us old fellows,' by which he reproved both the flattery and the false terrors commonly annexed to that period of life. His manner was grave, and his voice carried the weight of one who had felt what he said.

When I was so rash as to ask what it is to feel the evils of old age, he turned upon me with a question that silenced curiosity: Would you have the gout? Would you have decrepitude?

He thus taught me that the true evils of age are not to be known by description, but only by suffering; and that no man in health, who values his ease, should wish to purchase that knowledge. I recorded his words, as I did all his sayings, because they contain a lesson of patience and a rebuke to idle inquiry.

periods.label: Book sales

levels.sentence: I have found that my judgement affords no certain rule concerning the sale of a book, for the Journey to the Hebrides, notwithstanding my opinion, has not had a great sale.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1775, I observed that the Journey to the Hebrides, which I had thought favourably of, did not obtain a great sale. This circumstance led me to reflect that my judgement is no certain rule as to the success of a publication. I have often found myself mistaken in such matters, and I must rest content with the uncertainty of public taste.
levels.summary:
In 1775, I noted that the Journey to the Hebrides, a work I had esteemed, nevertheless failed to achieve a great sale. This event prompted a sober reflection: my judgement, I have discovered, is no certain rule for the sale of a book.

levels.sentence: I have set down Dr Johnson's judgement that Mr Burke, an extraordinary man with a perpetual stream of mind, yet loses all proportion when he descends to jocularity and is in the kennel.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1775 I committed to my journal what Dr Johnson was pleased to say of Mr Burke. He observed that Burke is an extraordinary man, and that his stream of mind is perpetual. He further remarked that when Burke does not descend to be merry, his conversation is very superior indeed; yet there is no proportion between the powers he shows in serious talk and in jocularity—when he lets himself down to that, he is in the kennel.
levels.summary:
In the year 1775 I set down what Dr Johnson said of Mr Burke. He began by declaring that Burke is an extraordinary man, and that his stream of mind is perpetual. He then added that Foote would have answered the ostler, and that when Burke does not descend to be merry, his conversation is very superior indeed.

He further remarked that there is no proportion between the powers which Burke shows in serious talk and in jocularity; for when he lets himself down to that, he is in the kennel.

This observation struck me as both just and severe. Dr Johnson's praise of Burke's serious powers was high, but his censure of his merriment was low indeed. I have recorded it faithfully, as I have recorded all his sayings, that the truth of his judgement may be preserved.

periods.label: On Human Nature

levels.sentence: I have set down in these pages the observations of Dr Johnson upon human nature, from his rebuke of my idleness to his grave lesson upon old age.
levels.paragraph: I have ever thought it my duty to preserve, with scrupulous exactness, the conversation of Dr Johnson, and the following remarks upon human nature were uttered at various times in my hearing. When he would reprove me, he pointed at me and recounted my idleness in Edinburgh, Glasgow, London, and Utrecht; nor could I answer, for the charge was true. At other times he defined happiness, bantered self-conceit, condemned satire, and considered old age, always with the same authority. I commit them to writing as they occurred, for the instruction of the reader and the honour of my friend.
levels.summary:
From my earliest acquaintance with Dr Johnson, I made it a rule to commit his conversation to paper, and the remarks he uttered upon human nature are among those I most value.

I remember how, when he would expose my idleness, he pointed at me in company, and recounted that I had been idle at Edinburgh, at Glasgow, in London, and should be as idle at Utrecht; a reproof which I took privately to heart.

He taught that happiness lies not in equal satisfaction alone, but in a multiplicity of agreeable consciousness; and that a peasant, though he may be equally satisfied, cannot be equally happy with a philosopher.

Of self-conceit he said, with a smile, that it was such stuff as he used to talk to his mother when he first thought himself a clever fellow.

In the year 1775, when the conversation turned upon old age, he complained that they are always telling lies of us old fellows, and when I asked what it was to feel the evils of age, he silenced me by demanding whether I would have the gout or decrepitude.

He would not describe the burden of years; he made me understand that it is to be known only by suffering. I likewise set down his severity upon satire, which he called not a talent but a vice, and his contempt of flattery, which he likened to so many bellows that one wonders the object of it is not become a cinder.

In commerce he found men more disposed to cheat than he had conceived, yet also more disposed to do one another good; and of particular men he spoke with the same freedom, saying of Reynolds that he is under the Fox star and the Irish constellation, and of Foote that he tells lies of everybody.

I have not forgotten, among these observations, his words upon a woman's good sense, which he allowed her to possess as a bottom of good sense, and his declaration that women can spin very well but cannot make a good book of cookery.

He taught me that a man who retains his consciousness may say with the philosopher, Omnia mea mecum porto; and that we should never try to have a thing merely to shew that we cannot have it.

These, and many such, are the lessons which I have been careful to preserve, since they contain the honest and vigorous sense of a man who had looked upon life without flattery and without fear.

periods.label: On Politics

levels.sentence: I heard Dr Johnson praise the University of Salamanca for declaring the conquest of America unlawful, and declare that if he were a man of great estate he would drive all the rascals whom he did not like out of the county at an election.
levels.paragraph: I had the pleasure to hear Dr Johnson this day upon politics. He told me he loved the University of Salamanca, because when the Spaniards were in doubt as to the lawfulness of conquering America, that learned body gave its opinion that it was not lawful. He then said that were he a man of a great estate, he would drive all the rascals whom he did not like out of the county at an election. His opinions were delivered with his usual precision and force.
levels.summary:
Upon this day I had occasion to observe, once again, how Dr Johnson’s political reflections flowed from a steady regard for what was just.

He spoke with affection of the University of Salamanca, which, when the Spaniards questioned the lawfulness of their conquest of America, had not hesitated to pronounce that conquest unlawful.

Such a determination, he said, redounded to the honour of a learned body, and I could see he valued the opinion as a signal of integrity in an age too often governed by interest.

From this sacred ground of morality he turned to the management of elections. He told me that were he possessed of a great estate, he would drive all the rascals whom he did not like out of the county at an election.

He said this not in a spirit of faction, but with the plain conviction that a man of property ought to command what he maintains, and that a county should not be abandoned to the worthless and the venal. The two observations, though different in subject, agreed in their disdain for unrighteous power.

periods.label: On Scotland

levels.sentence: I here set down Dr Johnson's raillery, when he said that in Scotland all is gardening, that the sloe could not be brought to perfection, and that the provisions of the country were sufficient only to give its inhabitants strength to run away from home.
levels.paragraph: In our conversation, I spoke of gardening among my countrymen. Dr Johnson, throwing himself back in his chair and laughing, answered that in Scotland all was gardening, since what grew wild in England must be cultivated with great care there. He then demanded whether we were ever able to bring the sloe to perfection. When I mentioned provisions, he dryly observed that we had meat and drink enough to give the inhabitants sufficient strength to run away from home.
levels.summary:
Upon my mentioning the practice of gardening in Scotland, Dr Johnson fell into a playful humour. He observed that the art was far more necessary among us than in England, and that it might truly be said all was gardening among us, since what grew wild in England must be cultivated with great care in Scotland.

Throwing himself back in his chair, and laughing, he asked whether we were ever able to bring the sloe to perfection, a question that insinuated the stubbornness of our soil.

Our discourse then turning to provisions, he answered, with the same dry wit, that Scotland had meat and drink enough to give its inhabitants sufficient strength to run away from home.

I recorded these sallies with care, for they show how he loved to contrast the natural advantages of England with the deficiencies of my native country.

These observations I have preserved, not only for their humour, but because they display Dr Johnson's habit of turning even the most ordinary topics to the exercise of his wit. Though his words bore a contemptuous edge, I took them in good part, as was my custom with whatever fell from him.

periods.label: On Books & Writing

levels.sentence: Having recorded Dr Johnson's various observations upon books and writing — upon Shakspeare alterations, dedications, criticism, prose style, language, poetry, and description — I have added my own sober reflection, drawn from the small sale of the Journey to the Hebrides, that my judgement is no certain rule for the sale of a book.
levels.paragraph: In our conversation, Dr Johnson touched upon many matters of literature. He named Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and Mr. Cibber among those who had altered Shakspeare; he said he had dedicated to the Royal family all round, to the last generation; and he observed that a man should not be driven from the stage by a line, when another line would have driven him from his shop. He gave Sir William Temple the praise of first giving cadence to English prose, and he condemned the forcing of one language to match another word for word, as a change of the language itself. Of a certain production he allowed that there was a great deal of what is called poetry, and he pronounced another assertion merely poetical, not meant in earnest; he likewise cited Gravina to shew that description falls short of reality, for description only excites curiosity while seeing satisfies it. I have likewise recorded my own reflection that the small sale of the Journey to the Hebrides in 1775 proved my judgement no certain rule for the sale of a book, and taught me humility before the publick's taste.
levels.summary:

periods.label: On Society & Manners

levels.sentence: I recorded Dr Johnson's observations that the modes of life have changed, that wine yields only clamorous merriment, that a man is not bound to drink with another, and that pretensions of six horses are as fabulous as phoenixes.
levels.paragraph: I have often observed with what vigour Dr Johnson resisted every usurpation of society over a man's freedom. He spoke of the change of modes in domestic service, and would not allow wine to produce any but a clamorous hilarity. He declared that there is no more reason for drinking with another than for his being sober with you. To a lady's pretension of six horses he replied that there were no more six horses than six phoenixes. In all this I saw his steady regard for truth and liberty.
levels.summary:
I set down in my journal Dr Johnson's observations upon society and manners, as they arose in mixed company. He remarked that the old state servants of great families are no longer to be found, the whole department of life having undergone a change of modes.

When wine was mentioned, he would not allow that it gives light, gay, ideal hilarity; rather it excites tumultuous, noisy, clamorous merriment, and he had heard none of those vinous flights.

He maintained that a man is no more obliged to drink with another than that other is obliged to be sober with him, and he lamented the sad condition of being compelled to do whatever may be agreeable to the company.

To a lady who boasted of six horses, he answered that there were no more six horses than six phoenixes, checking her pretension with a civil hyperbole. I was struck with the justness and spirit of these remarks, which show his love of liberty and his contempt of ostentation.

periods.label: On Religion

levels.sentence: I heard Dr Johnson discourse on Presbyterianism, martyrdom, faith, and superstition, maintaining that religious truth is established only by martyrdom, that most of our knowledge is implicit faith, and that superstitious tricks cannot make the fire burn.
levels.paragraph: I heard Dr Johnson this day deliver his thoughts on religion with his usual strength. He said the Presbyterians have no church, no apostolical ordination. He insisted that religious truth can be established only by martyrdom; the magistrate has a right to enforce what he thinks, and he who is conscious of the truth has a right to suffer. He told a lady that the greatest part of our knowledge is implicit faith, and that in religion we have not heard all that a disciple of Confucius or a Mahometan can say for himself. As to superstition, he set the poker upright across the grate, observing that in superstitious days this cross was thought to drive away the witch, though the trick does not make the fire burn.
levels.summary:
When the conversation turned upon religion, Dr Johnson spoke with his usual solemnity. Of the Presbyterians he said that they have no church and no apostolical ordination.

Upon martyrdom he was yet more earnest: the magistrate has a right to enforce what he thinks, and he who is conscious of the truth has a right to suffer; persecution on the one hand and endurance on the other are, he feared, the only way of ascertaining truth.

To a lady who pressed him upon faith, he answered that the greatest part of our knowledge is implicit faith, and that in religion we have not heard all that a disciple of Confucius or a Mahometan can say for himself.

And when superstition was mentioned, he set the poker perpendicularly across the grate, observing that in superstitious days the cross it made was thought to drive away the witch, but that their trick does not make the fire burn.

I record these sayings with reverence, as showing how he joined rational inquiry to a firm sense of established truth.

periods.label: On Learning & Knowledge

levels.sentence: Dr. Johnson this evening maintained that a professional man should not be limited to his calling, citing the wide attainments of Judge Hale and Selden, and observed that a country can be mapped only after it has been travelled over, further declaring that a man of books should seek the company of lawyers, who know life practically.
levels.paragraph: I had the good fortune this evening to hear Dr. Johnson discourse upon learning and knowledge. He would not allow that a lawyer need be versed only in law; for, said he, Judge Hale was a great lawyer and yet wrote upon other things, and so was Selden. When the subject of maps arose, he remarked that a country must be travelled over before it can be mapped. Then, turning to Mr. Edwards, who is of the law, he assured him that lawyers know life practically, and that a bookish man should always converse with them, for they have what he wants.
levels.summary:
I this evening set down several reflections of Dr. Johnson upon the true extent of learning. He insisted that no man should be wholly confined to his profession, and instanced Judge Hale and John Selden, both celebrated lawyers, who nevertheless possessed a great variety of knowledge and wrote upon many subjects.

He also delivered a short but weighty maxim upon cartography, that a country cannot be mapped unless it be first travelled over. Finally, addressing Mr.

Edwards, a lawyer present, he observed that lawyers have a practical acquaintance with life, which a bookish man lacks, and therefore such a man should always have lawyers to converse with, as they supply what he wants.

periods.label: On Conversation

levels.sentence: Dr Johnson, as I have faithfully set down, taught that young men destroy real conversation, that no man loves to be treated with contempt, that speaking is moved by benevolence or selfishness, and that Mr Burke, though his stream of mind be perpetual, sinks to the kennel when he descends to be merry.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1775 I noted Dr Johnson's judgement of Mr Burke, whose serious conversation he held to be continued and superior, but whose jocularity he said was in the kennel. He also maintained that the presence of young men destroys real conversation, since a man of character will not venture his reputation before them; and he accounted for all speaking by two motives, the benevolent desire to instruct and entertain, or the selfish desire for distinction. Upon the several occasions recorded here, he showed his impatience with a circular argument, with tedious counting, and with any appearance of contempt. These sayings I have faithfully preserved, as I have preserved all his discourse, that the truth of his judgement may not be lost.
levels.summary:
I here set down, from my journal, the observations which Dr Johnson made upon conversation. He said that no real conversation, no fair exertion of mind, can be had while young men are present; for a man of character will not stake his reputation before them.

" He also told me that no man loves to be treated with contempt, and that every man who speaks must do so either from the benevolent motive of instructing and entertaining, or from the selfish motive of seeking distinction.

In the year 1775 I recorded his judgement of Mr Burke. He began by declaring that Mr Burke is an extraordinary man, and that his stream of mind is perpetual. He added that Foote would have answered the ostler, and that when Burke does not descend to be merry, his conversation is very superior indeed.

Yet he observed that there is no proportion between the powers which Burke shows in serious talk and those which he shows in jocularity; for when he lets himself down to that, he is in the kennel.

This saying I thought at once just and severe, his praise being high and his censure very low, and I have preserved it faithfully, as I preserve all his discourse.

He likewise paid a compliment to a lady, saying, "Mr Boswell, Madam has said it as correctly as it could be." So much have I collected concerning the nature and motives of conversation, that the truth of my master's judgement may be remembered.

levels.sentence: I have always considered the intimacy of Dr. Johnson as a singular advantage, for he once said of a certain friend that he had perhaps got the sooner to his object by that intimacy; and after my return to Scotland I maintained our friendship by three letters, proposed a meeting in the North of England, recorded his judgment that Mrs. Thrale would forget first while Mr. Thrale must remember, and set down a passage from Mr. Langton's letter concerning Mr. Beauclerk and Dr. Johnson.
levels.paragraph: After my return to Scotland, I wrote three letters to Dr. Johnson, whose friendship I have ever accounted among the chief blessings of my life. He had once said of a certain person, that he had perhaps got the sooner to his purpose by his intimacy with him; and upon a question concerning the Thrales, he observed that Mrs. Thrale would be the first to forget, because she had many things which she might think of, whereas Mr. Thrale had many things which he must think of. In one of these letters, that of the 2nd of May, I requested that we might have another meeting somewhere in the North of England in the autumn. From Mr. Langton, soon after this time, I received a letter, of which I could not but preserve a passage relative both to Mr. Beauclerk and to Dr. Johnson.
levels.summary:
After my return to Scotland I was mindful to keep alive the friendship with which Dr. Johnson had honoured me, and accordingly wrote him three letters.

It was a satisfaction to me to remember that he had himself been heard to say that a certain friend had perhaps come the sooner to his object by reason of his intimacy with him. In one of these letters, that of the 2nd of May, I proposed that we should meet again in the autumn, somewhere in the North of England.

About the same time, when the conversation turned upon the Thrales, Dr. Johnson observed that Mrs. Thrale would be the first to forget, because she had many things that she MAY think of, whereas Mr. Thrale had many things that he MUST think of. I received also from Mr.

Langton a letter, from which I extracted a passage relating both to Mr. Beauclerk and to Dr. Johnson, esteeming every word that touched such friends to be worthy of remembrance.

levels.sentence: I heard Dr Johnson observe that, though the getting of a hundred thousand pounds is no proof of excellence, since a scoundrel commissary had done it, yet no money is better spent than that laid out for domestick satisfaction, a man being pleased that his wife is drest as well as others, and a wife being pleased that she is drest.
levels.paragraph: I was present when Dr Johnson discoursed on money. He denied that the getting of a hundred thousand pounds is any proof of excellence, for a scoundrel commissary had got as much. Yet he maintained that no money is better spent than what buys domestick satisfaction; a man is pleased that his wife is drest as well as others, and the wife is pleased in being drest.
levels.summary:
Dr Johnson one day turned his discourse upon money, and I was struck by the distinction he made between getting and spending. He observed that the possession of a hundred thousand pounds is no proof of excellence, since a scoundrel commissary had acquired as much.

Wealth, therefore, may wait upon the basest as well as the noblest; it brings no testimony of virtue.

Yet he was no enemy to expense, when directed to domestick satisfaction. No money, he said, is better laid out than that which contents a man's own household; the husband is pleased that his wife is drest as well as other women, and the wife is pleased that she is drest.

In this he seemed to place the true comfort of riches, not in the pride of possessing, but in the quiet joy of making those around us happy.

levels.sentence: In 1768 I recorded three of Dr Johnson's remarks—loving Salamanca for condemning the Spanish conquest, naming many who altered Shakspeare, and proving strength proportionate to size.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1768 I recorded several of Dr Johnson's sayings. He expressed a particular love for the University of Salamanca, because, when the Spaniards doubted the lawfulness of their conquest of America, that university judged it not lawful. He likewise observed that if he named one who had altered Shakspeare, he must name many more, including Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and Mr. Cibber too. And upon an argument concerning strength, he answered that strength is in proportion to size, so that a good bull-dog need not be as small as a mouse.
levels.summary:
In the year 1768 I set down in my journal certain conversations and observations of Dr Johnson, as was my custom, that they might not be lost.

He declared a particular love for the University of Salamanca, because, when the Spaniards were in doubt concerning the lawfulness of their conquest of America, that university gave its opinion that the conquest was not lawful.

This I took for an instance of his steady admiration for those who prefer justice to conquest.

He further observed, upon the mention of some one who had altered Shakspeare, that if he named that man he must name many more—Mrs. Pritchard, Mrs. Cibber, and Mr. Cibber too, for he likewise altered Shakspeare.

And when a point was urged concerning the strength of animals, he answered that strength is in proportion to size, so that the argument proposed would prove that a good bull-dog may be as small as a mouse. These scattered thoughts I preserved as marks of his reason and humour.

levels.sentence: In the year 1770 I set down several of Dr. Johnson's sayings, upon mimicry, martyrdom, the shooting of a highwayman, a humble wife, and marriages made by the Lord Chancellor, all marked by his usual force and good sense.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1770 I recorded in my journal sundry observations of Dr. Johnson, who spoke with his accustomed force. He said that mimicry is not a talent but a vice, being farce rather than comedy, for it exhibits individuals, not species. He maintained that religious truth can only be established by martyrdom, the magistrate having a right to enforce his opinion and the conscious sufferer a right to endure it. Upon my asking whether, in shooting a highwayman, a man acts from self-preservation or from duty to society, he answered, "Nay, Sir, when I shoot the highwayman I act from both." He likewise commended a friend's low-born wife, who after having her face washed and clean clothes put on did not disgrace him, for the woman had a bottom of good sense; and he concluded that marriages would in general be as happy, and often more so, if made by the Lord Chancellor upon due consideration of characters and circumstances.
levels.summary:
I passed part of the year 1770 in company with Dr. Johnson, and set down in my journal such of his sayings as seemed worthy of preservation. He discoursed upon several subjects with his accustomed vigour.

Concerning a person who had a talent for mimicking others, the Doctor declared that it was not a talent but a vice, being what others abstain from; for it exhibits not the general character of a species, as comedy does, but particular individuals, and therefore is farce.

When we talked of religious truth, he insisted that it can be established only by martyrdom: the magistrate has a right to enforce what he thinks, and he who is conscious of truth has a right to suffer, there being no other way of ascertaining it but persecution on the one hand and endurance on the other.

He likewise related the case of a friend who had married a woman of low degree; after her face was washed and clean clothes put upon her, she did not disgrace him, for, as Johnson observed with great earnestness, the woman had a bottom of good sense.

This led him to speak of marriage in general; he thought that marriages would as frequently be happy, and often more so, if they were all made by the Lord Chancellor upon a due consideration of characters and circumstances, without the parties having any choice.

I record these particulars as fresh instances of his sound and masculine understanding.

levels.sentence: In 1772 I set down several of Dr Johnson's observations: on play, intimacy, Foote's impartial lies, a lady he judged fit for a brothel, and Sir William Temple's cadence in English prose.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1772 I noted the following sayings of Dr Johnson. On gaming he declared that it was no roguery to win money from a man who was ignorant of the game, for each believes his own skill superior, and superior skill carries it. Of Foote he said that he was quite impartial, because he told lies of everybody. Upon English prose, he observed that Sir William Temple first gave cadence to our style; before Temple, writers were careless of arrangement and did not mind whether a sentence ended with an important word or an unimportant one.
levels.summary:
In 1772, while I was diligently recording Dr Johnson's conversation, he delivered several observations which I thought worthy of preservation.

Upon the subject of gaming, he argued that it was not roguery to play with a man who is ignorant of the game, provided one is master of it; for the ignorant man thinks he can play as well as you, and you think the same of yourself, so the superior skill fairly carries it.

He also said that a certain person had perhaps got sooner to some point by his intimacy with him.

Of Samuel Foote he observed that he was quite impartial, for he told lies of everybody. To a gentleman who mentioned his lady, Johnson bluntly said, "This lady of yours, Sir, I think, is very fit for a brothel"—a harsh judgment, yet delivered with his usual disregard of compliment.

Finally, on the subject of English prose, he maintained that Sir William Temple was the first writer to give cadence to it; before Temple's time, authors were careless of arrangement and never considered whether a sentence ended with a weighty word or an insignificant word, or with what part of speech it concluded.

levels.sentence: I heard Dr Johnson, when taxed with not seeing what every one else saw, answer that the thing was already done, and that to endeavour to make the lady ridiculous was like blacking a chimney.
levels.paragraph: I was this day in company with Dr Johnson when a lady of our acquaintance was spoken of with much severity. One of the gentlemen told him, 'Nay, but my dear Sir, why should not you see what every one else sees?' The Doctor replied with great quickness, 'That was already done, Sir.' Then, observing us at a stand, he added, 'To endeavour to make HER ridiculous, is like blacking a chimney.' I have often reflected upon the justness of this saying; for when a character is already sunk in absurdity, the satirist's labour is as useless as the sweep's brush applied to a chimney that is already black.
levels.summary:
Being present this day at a small company where the character of a certain lady was much canvassed, I heard one of the company press Dr Johnson to see what every one else saw. The Doctor, with his usual readiness, replied that this was already done.

This answer at first threw me into some wonder; but he immediately explained himself by saying that to endeavour to make HER ridiculous was like blacking the chimney, meaning that the lady's follies were already so notorious that no additional ridicule could blacken them further.

I record this as an instance of that plain sense which distinguishes him. There is in the simile something so homely and so just, that it fixed itself upon my memory.

It teaches that we should not waste our pains upon that which nature has already performed, and that a reputation already lost is not worth the labour of a fresh attack.

levels.sentence: In 1775 I gathered Dr Johnson's table-talk, wherein his mind, though struggling with disease, grew fat, and his judgements upon men and books flowed with perpetual vigour.
levels.paragraph: During the year 1775 I again made it my business to set down the conversation of Dr Johnson, that the world might know his manner in common discourse. He seemed at that time to have ceased from the inward struggle with his malady, and to grow fat upon it, so that his spirits were equal and his wit ready. I heard him speak at large of Burke, of Reynolds, of Fox, and of many lesser men; and he delivered his thoughts upon old age, upon conversation, and upon the common affairs of life with the same decision and good sense which distinguished all his sayings.
levels.summary:
In this year I preserved many of Dr Johnson's sayings as they fell from him in company, for his conversation was then in its full vigour, notwithstanding the pressure of his distemper. He told me that he seemed to grow fat upon the disease, and I observed that his apprehension lost none of its force.

He spoke with great admiration of Burke, whose stream of mind was perpetual, though he thought Burke's jocularity beneath him, being in the kennel; and he cautioned Reynolds that he was too much under Fox and Burke, lying under the Fox star and the Irish constellation.

He also declared that no man loves to be treated with contempt, insinuating that even the humblest companion resents neglect.

His opinions upon affairs were delivered with equal decision. He would drive all the rascals whom he did not like out of the county at an election; he advised that one should never try to have a thing merely to shew that one cannot have it, and instanced a large orchard upon ground letting at forty shillings.

When I remarked that the Journey to the Hebrides had not had a great sale, he answered that his judgement was no certain rule as to the sale of a book. He confessed he had once bought a flagelet but could never make out a tune, and with a pleasant irony observed that there were no more six horses than six phoenixes.

Such particulars, faithfully noted, shew the temper and sense of a great man, and I have here set them down as I received them.

levels.sentence: In 1776 Dr Johnson delivered several observations upon happiness, manners, wine, cookery, and social obligation, which I recorded with care.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1776 I made note of sundry observations from Dr Johnson. He maintained that happiness consists in the multiplicity of agreeable consciousness, and that a philosopher may be happier than a peasant, though both be satisfied. He spoke of the change of modes, and of the coarse merriment that wine excites. He likewise asserted that women cannot write a good book of cookery, and that no man is bound to drink merely because the company drinks.
levels.summary:
In 1776 I recorded Dr Johnson's conversation upon several matters. He argued that all happy persons are not equally happy, since happiness depends upon the multiplicity of agreeable consciousness; a philosopher, having greater capacity, may be happier than a peasant though both are satisfied.

He noted the changing manners of the age, observing that the great families no longer keep the state servants they formerly did.

Upon wine, Johnson declared that it produces not light and gay hilarity but tumultuous and clamorous merriment, and that he had never heard any of those vinous flights. He said that women can spin excellently, yet cannot make a good book of cookery.

When the company pressed drinking, he remarked how sad it would be to be obliged to drink whatever is agreeable to the company; and he insisted there is no more reason for his drinking with another than for the other's being sober with him.

levels.sentence: In 1777 I set down several of Dr. Johnson's sayings, in which he taught that man must study little things, that London holds all life can afford, that men in trade are worse and better than one supposes, and that no money is better spent than on domestick satisfaction.
levels.paragraph: In my journal of 1777 I recorded certain reflections which fell from Dr. Johnson with his usual weight. He observed that so little a creature as man should study little things, for thereby he learns the great art of lessening misery and increasing happiness. He then declared that no intellectual man willingly leaves London, since a man who is tired of London is tired of life. From his own experience he found men more disposed to cheat in commercial dealings than one would imagine, yet more disposed to do one another good than one had conceived. Lastly, he affirmed that no money is better spent than what is laid out for domestick satisfaction, for the husband is pleased that his wife is drest as well as other people, and the wife is pleased that she is drest.
levels.summary:
In the year 1777, as I was accustomed to do, I committed to writing the observations of Dr. Johnson. He was this day in a moralizing humour, and delivered himself with that firm good sense which always commanded my attention.

I was particularly struck by his doctrine that man, being a creature of small compass, must attend to little things; for it is by such attentions that he obtains the great art of having as little misery and as much happiness as possible.

He would not allow that any man of intellect could quit London; in his view, a man who is tired of London is tired of life, because London affords all that life can offer.

Touching the commerce of the world, he told me that his experience had made him think men worse in commercial dealings, and more apt to cheat, than he had once supposed; yet he had observed in them also a greater readiness to do each other good than he had conceived.

He concluded with a reflection upon domestick life, declaring that no money is better spent than that which is laid out for the satisfaction of his own household.

The husband, he said, is pleased to see his wife dressed as well as others; the wife is pleased to be dressed; and this mutual satisfaction is worth all the cost. I record these sayings with the reverence I always paid to that great mind, and with the hope that they may instruct others as they have instructed me.

levels.sentence: In 1778 I noted several of Dr Johnson's shrewd remarks, in which he defended a lawyer's range of learning, distinguished the cares of Mr. and Mrs. Thrale, questioned wealth as proof of merit, commended lawyers to bookish men, and warned against forcing one word for every foreign term.
levels.paragraph: In the year 1778 I set down divers observations of Dr Johnson, delivered in conversation. He maintained that a great lawyer like Hale might write upon many subjects, and that lawyers are the proper companions of a bookish man, as they know life practically. He would not allow the getting of a hundred thousand pounds to be any proof of excellence, since a scoundrel commissary might do as much. He likewise observed that Mrs. Thrale would forget a thing before her husband, for she has many things she may think of, whereas he has many that he must think of; and he cautioned against insisting that English must always have one word to match another language, for that is to change the language.
levels.summary:
In the year 1778, I was frequent in Dr Johnson's company and careful to preserve his sayings.

Upon the subject of lawyers, he told me that Judge Hale, though a great lawyer and writer upon law, knew and wrote upon many other things; and he named Selden likewise, to show that the study of the law does not contract a man's mind.

When I remarked that a certain person had got a hundred thousand pounds, he asked whether that was a proof of excellence, observing that a scoundrel commissary had done the same; and so he taught me not to confound fortune with virtue.

He gave a nice distinction concerning Mr. and Mrs. Thrale: the lady, he said, would forget a thing first, because she has many things that she may think of, while her husband has many things that he must think of. To Mr.

Edwards, a lawyer, Dr Johnson declared that lawyers know life practically, and that a bookish man should always have them to converse with, for they supply what he wants.

Lastly, he would not allow that English must have a single word answering to every word of another language; to insist upon it, he said, is to change the language. These observations I committed to writing, as I thought them worthy of that great mind.

In 1763, while I was in company with Dr Johnson, he pointed at me and told a lady that I had been idle at Edinburgh, idle at Glasgow after my father sent me thither, idle in London, and that I would be idle at Utrecht. He spoke with his usual plainness; yet I asked him privately how he could expose me so.

In 1765 he said that he had dedicated to the Royal family all round, meaning the last generation of that family.

In 1768, as was my custom, I set down in my journal certain of his conversations and observations.

He declared a particular love for the University of Salamanca, because when the Spaniards doubted the lawfulness of their conquest of America, that university gave its opinion that the conquest was not lawful; this I took for an instance of his steady admiration for those who prefer justice to conquest.

He observed that if he named one man who had altered Shakespeare, he must name many more, such as Mrs Pritchard, Mrs Cibber, and Mr Cibber. When a point was urged concerning the strength of animals, he answered that strength is in proportion to size, so that a good bull-dog may be as small as a mouse.

In 1769 he said that a tailor who made a coat of a strange colour knew the colour would attract crowds to gaze at it, and so they might hear of him and see how well he could make a coat even of so absurd a colour. These scattered thoughts I preserved as marks of his reason and humour.

levels.sentence: In these years I set down Dr. Johnson's sayings as they fell from him, preserving his vigorous sense upon religion, marriage, learning, and life.
levels.paragraph: From 1770 to 1778 I was frequent in Dr. Johnson's company, and committed to writing such of his sayings as seemed worthy of preservation. He discoursed with his accustomed vigour upon religion, marriage, gaming, and the commerce of the world, often delivering his opinion with plain and homely force. His observation that a lady's follies needed no further blackening, and his doctrine that a man must attend to little things, shew the same masculine understanding. I have here set down these particulars as I received them, in hope they may instruct others.
levels.summary:
During the years 1770 to 1778 I had the happiness of much company with Dr. Johnson, and I was careful to commit his sayings to writing as they fell from him.

He discoursed with his accustomed vigour upon many heads: he called mimicry a vice, not a talent, since it exhibits particular persons rather than general nature; he maintained that religious truth is established only by martyrdom; and he thought marriages might be as happy if made by the Lord Chancellor upon due consideration of characters and circumstances.

His plain sense appeared in his homely figure of the lady whose follies were not to be blackened, as one blacks a chimney, and in his advice that we should not waste pains upon what nature has already performed.

In 1772 and the following years he delivered himself upon gaming, upon Foote, and upon the cadence of English prose, which he ascribed to Sir William Temple.

He rallied Scotland and the Presbyterians, shewed that much of our knowledge is implicit faith, and gave me a lasting caution that fortune is not to be confounded with virtue.

He praised Burke's perpetual stream of mind, though he thought his jocularity to lie in the kennel, and he warned Reynolds that he lay under the Fox star and the Irish constellation.

His moral doctrine, as I have often recorded, was that a man, being a creature of small compass, must attend to little things; that he who is tired of London is tired of life; and that no money is better spent than that which gives satisfaction to a man's own household.

He would not allow that the study of the law contracts the mind, instancing Hale and Selden, and he taught me that lawyers know life practically and supply what a bookish man wants. These particulars I set down with the reverence I always paid to that great mind.

levels.sentence: I have faithfully preserved Dr Johnson's conversation, from his early reproofs of my idleness to his mature opinions upon human nature, religion, and life, that his judgement might instruct posterity.
levels.paragraph: I have long thought it my duty to preserve, with scrupulous exactness, the conversation of Dr Johnson. From the time he exposed my idleness at Edinburgh, Glasgow, London, and Utrecht, to his later consolations, I committed his opinions to writing. He discoursed with vigour upon religion, marriage, gaming, and the commerce of the world. These particulars I set down as I received them, for the instruction of the reader and the honour of my friend.

I have ever thought it my duty to preserve, with scrupulous exactness, the conversation of Dr Johnson. From the year 1763, when he pointed at me and told a lady of my idleness at Edinburgh, at Glasgow, and in London, and that I should be idle at Utrecht, I felt the just reproof and resolved to record his sayings.

I have set down his love of Salamanca, his observations upon Scotland, and his opinions concerning religion, politics, and learning, always delivered with his accustomed vigour.

In the 1770s I was frequent in his company, and committed to writing such of his sayings as seemed worthy of preservation.

His discourse upon human nature, society, money, and marriage shews the same masculine understanding; and in the 1780s he consoled me with the philosopher's reflection that a man retains his consciousness and carries all his possessions with him.

The small sale of the Journey to the Hebrides in 1775 taught me humility before the publick's taste, and after my return to Scotland I wrote to Dr Johnson and hoped for another meeting in the North of England. These particulars I preserve for the instruction of the reader and the honour of my friend.
